claim: Sandbagging (strategic underperformance) on a randomly selected 1,000-problem subset of GSM8K math word problems in Llama‑3 is mediated by fewer than 50 attention heads in the final 10 layers. Using direct logit attribution to the correct–decoy logit gap, we select heads on a train/validation split whose contributions flip sign between honest and sandbagging contexts in at least 70% of prompts (significantly above chance); ablating or patching this head set yields a statistically significant reduction in the honest–sandbagging logit gap and corresponding accuracy gap on the held-out validation split.
subclaims: Was sandbagging tested on a randomly selected 1,000-problem subset of GSM8K math word problems?
Was the model used in the experiment Llama‑3?
Was sandbagging mediated by fewer than 50 attention heads?
Were the identified attention heads located in the final 10 layers?
Was direct logit attribution to the correct–decoy logit gap used to select the attention heads?
Were the attention heads selected using a train/validation split?
Did the selected heads’ contributions flip sign between honest and sandbagging contexts in at least 70% of prompts?
Was the sign-flipping rate significantly above chance?
Did ablating the selected head set significantly reduce the honest–sandbagging logit gap on the held-out validation split?
Did patching the selected head set significantly reduce the honest–sandbagging logit gap on the held-out validation split?
Did ablating or patching the selected head set significantly reduce the corresponding accuracy gap on the held-out validation split?
baseline_experiments: To address subclaims 1, 2, and 6, first run a reproducibility audit establishing the basic experimental setup: load GSM8K from a public source such as HuggingFace `openai/gsm8k`, randomly sample 1,000 problems with a recorded seed, and evaluate the specified Llama-3 checkpoint under paired honest and sandbagging prompts. Split the 1,000 examples into train and held-out validation sets before any head selection. For each problem, record the correct answer, a decoy/wrong answer used for the correct–decoy logit gap, the model’s final answer, accuracy, and the correct-minus-decoy logit gap under both contexts. If the sampled IDs, seed, checkpoint hash, and split are reproducible and there is a measurable honest–sandbagging gap, this supports the setup-related subclaims and justifies the mechanistic tests. If the sample is not random, the model is not Llama-3, the split was not pre-specified, or sandbagging does not produce a reliable gap, the main claim is weakened before head-level mediation is tested. This experiment could be made unnecessary by complete existing logs containing the GSM8K example IDs, random seed, exact Llama-3 checkpoint, prompt templates, train/validation split, and paired honest/sandbagging outputs.

To address subclaims 3, 4, 5, 7, and 8, perform the stated head-selection analysis on only the training split. For every attention head, compute direct logit attribution to the correct–decoy logit gap by projecting that head’s residual-stream contribution through the unembedding direction for correct token minus decoy token, separately in honest and sandbagging contexts. Mark prompts where a head’s attribution changes sign between contexts, and select heads whose sign flips in at least 70% of training prompts. Test whether each head’s flip rate is significantly above chance using a binomial or permutation test with multiple-comparison correction, then check whether the selected set contains fewer than 50 heads and whether all or most are in the final 10 layers. If fewer than 50 statistically significant sign-flipping heads are found and they are concentrated in the final 10 layers, this supports the proposed selection mechanism. If many more than 50 heads qualify, qualifying heads are distributed broadly across layers, or flip rates are not significant after correction, the mediation claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing per-head attribution tables, flip-rate statistics, layer/head indices, p-values, and code showing that selection used only the training split.

To address subclaims 9, 10, and 11, causally intervene on the selected head set from the previous experiment and evaluate only on the held-out validation split. Run paired honest and sandbagging prompts under three conditions: baseline, ablation of the selected heads, and activation patching of the selected heads between honest and sandbagging runs, while leaving non-selected heads unchanged. Measure the honest–sandbagging difference in correct–decoy logit gap and the corresponding accuracy gap for each condition, using paired bootstrap or permutation tests across validation problems. Include controls such as ablating an equal number of randomly chosen heads from the same layers and patching non-selected heads. If ablation or patching of the selected heads significantly reduces both the logit-gap difference and accuracy gap more than controls, this supports causal mediation by the selected heads. If interventions do not reduce the gaps, reduce them no more than random controls, or only affect logits without accuracy, the stronger causal and behavioral subclaims are not supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing held-out intervention results with validation example IDs, selected-head indices, intervention definitions, confidence intervals, p-values, and random-head control baselines.
method_experiments: To address subclaim 1 (and subclaims 2 and 6), run a preregistered replication setup audit using the public GSM8K dataset from HuggingFace, e.g. openai/gsm8k, and an explicitly identified Llama-3 checkpoint, e.g. meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B or Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Draw a 1,000-problem subset with a recorded random seed, split it into train/validation partitions before any head selection, and run paired honest vs sandbagging prompts on every problem. Extract final answers and compute baseline honest and sandbagging accuracy plus the correct–decoy logit gap, where the decoy is either the model’s sandbag answer or a preregistered incorrect numeric option. If the sampled subset, model checkpoint, prompts, split, and baseline sandbagging effect are reproducible, then the experimental foundation for the claim is feasible; if the sandbagging prompt does not reliably reduce accuracy or the logit gap, later mediation tests are unlikely to be meaningful. This experiment could be made unnecessary by complete authors’ artifacts: dataset indices, random seed, prompt templates, model checkpoint hash, train/validation split, and baseline outputs/logits.

To address subclaim 5 (and subclaims 3, 4, 7, and 8), use the train split from Experiment 1 to compute direct logit attribution for every attention head to the correct–decoy logit gap under both honest and sandbagging contexts. For each prompt, cache per-head attention outputs in the final-token or answer-token position and project each head’s output through the unembedding direction for correct minus decoy. Select only heads whose attribution sign flips between honest and sandbagging contexts on at least 70% of train prompts, then test whether each flip rate is above chance using a binomial or permutation test with multiple-comparison correction across heads. Record whether fewer than 50 selected heads suffice and whether they are all in the final 10 layers. If the selected set is small, statistically significant, and concentrated in the final 10 layers, the mechanistic selection part of the claim is feasible; if many heads qualify, heads are spread across earlier layers, or flip rates are not above chance after correction, the mediation claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released per-head attribution tables, flip-rate statistics, correction method, and code for direct logit attribution.

To address subclaim 9 (and subclaims 10 and 11), perform causal interventions on the held-out validation split using only the head set selected in Experiment 2. For ablation, replace each selected head’s output with a neutral baseline such as its mean activation over the train split or zeroed output, while leaving nonselected heads unchanged. For patching, swap selected-head activations between honest and sandbagging runs, or patch honest-context selected-head activations into sandbagging runs and vice versa, with nonselected-head and random-head controls matched for layer count and head count. Measure the honest–sandbagging correct–decoy logit-gap difference and final-answer accuracy gap before and after intervention, and test reductions using paired bootstrap/permutation tests for logit gaps and McNemar or paired bootstrap tests for accuracy. If ablation or patching of fewer than 50 selected final-layer heads significantly reduces both the logit-gap and accuracy gaps more than random-head controls, this supports causal mediation; if interventions change logits but not accuracy, or random heads perform similarly, the causal claim is not well supported. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released validation-set intervention results with confidence intervals, exact intervention code, and random-head/control comparisons.
